citeinfo.title: Whooping crane stopover habitat use and migration movement data in relation to drought severity, 2010-2022

descript.abstract: Wildlife species face threats from climate and land use change, which may exacerbate how extreme climatic events influence population persistence and biodiversity. Migratory waterbirds are especially vulnerable to hydrological drought via reduced availability of surface water habitats. We assessed how whooping cranes, an endangered species in the U.S. and Canada, modified habitat use and migration strategies during drought to understand this species’ resilience to changing conditions and adaptive capacity. The data included 8,555 night-roost sites used by 145 cranes, 2010–2022, under non-drought conditions, moderate drought, and extreme drought conditions.
descript.purpose: Assess differences in night-roost habitats used and movements by migrating whooping cranes across the Great Plains and Boreal Transition Zones in the midcontinent of North America.

method.methdesc: During 2009–2022, we captured whooping cranes at sites along coastal Texas and in and around Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada and marked them with leg-mounted transmitters capable of collecting locations using global position system (GPS) capabilities and transmitting data using platform transmitting terminals (North Star Science and Technology LLC, Baltimore, MD, United States; Geotrak, Inc., Apex, NC, United States) or Global System for Mobiles (GSM) and Global Packet Radio Service (GPRS) third and fourth generation cellular networks (Ornitela, Vilnius, Lithuania). We used helicopters to locate pre-fledged juveniles at breeding sites in Canada and captured individuals by hand. At wintering sites in Texas, we captured adult and juvenile cranes with modified leg snares. Marking and capture were conducted under Federal Fish and Wildlife Permit TE048806, Texas research permit SPR-1112-1042, Aransas National Wildlife Refuge special use permit, Environment and Climate Change Canada Scientific Permits to Capture and Band Migratory Birds 10827 and 10915, Environment and Climate Change Canada Scientific permits NWT-SCI-10-04, NWT/AB/SK/MB-SCI-16-01, SC-NR-2019-NT-002, SC-NR-2022-NT-001, Parks Canada Agency Research and Collection Permits WB-2010-4998, WB-2017-23857, WB-2019-31922, WB-2022-41918, Northwest Territories Wildlife Care Committee permits NWTWCC 2010-008, NWTWCC 2017-012, NWTWCC 2019-010, and NWTWCC 2022-003 and Northwest Territories Wildlife Research Permits WL004807, WL004821, and WL500051, WL500516, WL500726, and WL501043. Procedures were approved by Animal Care and Use Committee at Northern Prairie Wildlife Research Center and Environment and Climate Change Canada’s Animal Care Committees.

procstep.procdesc:
We used location data from individual whooping cranes, collected in the study area during spring (inter-quartile range [IQR] = 4 Apr–23 Apr) and autumn (IQR = 8 Oct–5 Nov) migration seasons, 2010–2022. For each crane, we extracted one roost location per night (location closest to 00:00 Central Standard Time Zone) that was classified as occurring on the ground (instantaneous velocity reading <2.6 m/s). Nightly roost locations were further collapsed across all sequential locations occurring on the same surface water body or reach of a river. We characterized locations into seven categories of roosting habitat. We used wetland classification systems to assist where available and satellite and aerial imagery. Aerial imagery was accessed across several decades via Google Earth Pro version 7.3 using the “time slider” tool, which aided in confirming wetland presence and classification. We identified ownership of locations using the Protected Areas Database or the Canadian Protected and Conserved Areas Database. Finally, we noted if locations occurred within areas designated as critical habitat for migrating whooping cranes. We identified unique stopovers sites as those with ≥1 collapsed nightly location within 15 km of each other. Using stopover site designations, we calculated residency time and distance between stopover sites within the area of study.
We compiled information on status of drought for roost sites used by whooping cranes from the U.S. (Source 1) and Canada (Source 2) drought monitor systems, which use multiple assessment indices to characterize soil moisture, streamflow, and precipitation. We downloaded spatial vector digital data from the month of April to represent spring migration and October to represent autumn migration. In the U.S., drought data were available each week; we used information from the middle of each month to characterize status of seasonal drought. Both drought classifications used a five-category system to characterize drought status across each nation. We collapsed these categories to form three levels of drought severity. Locations with no drought designation or identified as “D0-abnormally dry” were identified as non-drought condition. Locations identified as “D1-moderate” or “D2-severe” drought were identified as moderate drought conditions. Finally, we identified locations in “D3-extreme” or “D4-exceptional” drought as experiencing extreme drought conditions.

edom.edomvd: Palustrine wetlands. Included shallow emergent and open water wetlands.

Palustrine agricultural wetlands. Palustrine wetlands within cultivated fields, with limited hydrophytes, and a history of cultivation across the entirety of the wetland basin, which we assessed using aerial imagery.
Impounded palustrine wetland. Any palustrine wetland that was modified to increase wetland hydroperiod (i.e., impounded, excavated, or diked).
Lacustrine wetlands. Primarily deep-water wetlands >8 ha in size or deeper than 2.5 m at low water with <30% coverage of vegetation.
River. Lotic systems of all flooding frequencies.
Uplands. Non-wetland locations located generally in grasslands or cultivated lands.
